There is thus no evidence, genetic or biological, linking AMY2B variation or function to schizophrenia, making "Novel" the appropriate designation.

None of the provided articles mention schizophrenia at all; the literature set is dominated by AOC3/VAP-1 (SSAO) biology in inflammation, leukocyte trafficking, adipose tissue, diabetes, colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and enzymology. There are no human genetic association or variant studies linking AOC3 to schizophrenia, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. Weak indirect biological plausibility exists because AOC3 is a copper amine oxidase that oxidizes primary amines including dopamine and methylamine, and AOC3 levels change with dopamine replacement therapy in Parkinson's disease (PMIDs 22238597, 42401611), which could support a speculative monoamine/neuroinflammation link. However, these are co-mentions of neurotransmitter biology rather than any schizophrenia-relevant evidence, so the weight falls mostly on Novel with some allowance for Hypothesized.

Two human genetic studies report direct association: an imaging-genetics genome-wide screen using DLPFC BOLD activation as a quantitative phenotype that identified ARHGAP18 SNPs and corroborated the case–control distribution in an independent sample (PMID 19065146), and a Chinese Han case–control study of >2000 subjects with a validation cohort reporting SNPs rs7758025/rs9483050 (PMID 28384650). A review (PMID 20600988) restates these findings and places ARHGAP18 in neurodevelopmental gene networks, which is background/citation rather than independent evidence. The remaining articles concern endothelial, aortic, corneal, and YAP/RhoC biology, or unrelated vasculitis genetics, and do not bear on schizophrenia. Because the association rests essentially on modest, ethnicity-specific cohorts with limited independent replication and no confirmation in large psychiatric GWAS, the evidence supports "Existing" rather than "Established."

None of the provided articles studies Autism Spectrum Disorder directly; there are no ASD cohorts, probands, or families reporting ARHGAP18 variants, so Established and Existing are effectively unsupported. The strongest neuro-relevant human data are association of ARHGAP18 SNPs with schizophrenia in Han Chinese and in imaging-genetics GWAS using DLPFC activation (PMIDs 28384650, 19065146, 20600988), plus differential methylation/expression in monozygotic twins discordant for IQ (PMID 23082141) — these implicate the gene in neurodevelopment and cognition, phenotypes adjacent to but not equivalent to ASD. The remainder of the literature concerns endothelial senescence, aortic disease, microtubule stability, YAP signalling and tumorigenesis, i.e., non-neural biology (PMIDs 28251925, 24334613, 32013974, 25778702). This supports a plausible biological/pathway rationale (RhoGTPase regulation, cortical progenitor proliferation and migration) rather than direct genetic evidence, so Hypothesized receives the most weight, with substantial probability remaining for Novel given the absence of any ASD-specific mention.

No article in this set reports variants in ANKFN1 in schizophrenia patients, so Established is untenable (no PMIDs demonstrate probands or families with causal variants). The only human genetic study (PMID 21668797) is a GWAS of DSM-IV cannabis dependence in which ANKFN1 SNPs gave the top, sub-genome-wide-significant signals; cannabis dependence is an environmental risk factor associated with psychosis, which gives weak, indirect support for "Existing," but the association is neither schizophrenia itself nor statistically definitive. The remaining papers (PMIDs 35100349, 36533556) are zebrafish/Drosophila/mouse studies of vestibular and ciliary function; they show neurological roles for Ankfn1 but do not link it to schizophrenia biology in a specific way, providing only a thin basis for "Hypothesized." Overall, the co-mentions are largely incidental, so Novel receives the largest share with meaningful weight also on Existing and Hypothesized.

Human genetic association studies of the EGF A61G (rs4444903) polymorphism report a case–control association with schizophrenia in Finnish men (PMID 15129177), and multiple independent samples report a sex-specific effect on age at onset in males (PMIDs 16115648, 16979250), plus a gene–gene interaction with TNFα affecting onset age (PMID 15614591). However, replication for disease risk is inconsistent, with clearly negative case-control studies in Japanese (PMID 15729146) and Korean (PMID 15663953) populations, and a recent review concluding EGF rs4444903 shows no consistent risk association (PMID 42390996). Supporting biology is strong but non-genetic: reduced EGF protein in postmortem prefrontal cortex/striatum and serum (PMID 12192610), altered EGF pathway gene expression in BA46 (PMID 39242583), and mixed serum biomarker findings (PMIDs 32300175, 15993491). This mixture of at least one credible human genetic association plus replicated modifier (age-at-onset) effects, without definitive causal replication, fits "Existing"; residual probability goes to "Hypothesized" given that much of the evidence is expression/biomarker-based.

One human genetic association study (PMID 17626784) reported haplotypic association of EGF SNPs with autism in 252 AGRE trios, which constitutes credible but single, unreplicated variant-level evidence — sufficient for "Existing" but not "Established". Supporting but non-genetic human evidence includes repeatedly reduced plasma/serum EGF in children and adults with ASD (PMIDs 22937258, 17123472, 23645980, 34062079) and cord blood/maternal immune profiling implicating EGF (PMIDs 39163910, 34987169), plus transcriptomic evidence of diminished EGF signaling in ASD blood (PMID 27862943). These are biomarker/expression findings rather than genetic causation, so a substantial share of probability remains with "Hypothesized". Other EGF articles concern breast/endometrial cancer, Alzheimer's, or ADPKD and are irrelevant, while NRG2/NRG3/MEGF10 papers only mention EGF-like domains, not the EGF gene itself.

A weak indirect neuro-link comes from ELL's implication in an Alzheimer disease TWAS/fly model (40215969) and general transcription-elongation/YEATS-domain connections to neurodevelopmental disorders (35279775), which could support a speculative "hypothesized" mechanism but not a schizophrenia-specific one. Overall the evidence base is dominated by incidental co-mention, so Novel is most probable, with some weight to Hypothesized given plausible neurodevelopmental transcription-regulation biology.
